What is it?: Survival horror submerged in Lovecraft's 1920s. Expect to pay: £41.35/$50 Developer: Frogwares Publisher: Frogwares Reviewed on: Windows 11, Intel Core i9, 32GB RAM, Nvidia RTX 4060 Multiplayer?: No Steam Deck: Unknown Out: August 18 Link: Official site

The Sinking City was exactly the kind of ambitious but flawed game that deserves a sequel. Good ideas, middling execution? Give 'em another shot, I'm sure they'll do better second time around. What was ambitious was that it was a detective game but also a horror game about H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos set in a flooded open world where sometimes you have to get around by motorboating, and not in the fun way.

Fine idea, but it suffered from the classic open world problem of not enough butter spread across too much toast, quickly repeating patterns that become so familiar they were robbed of mystery and spookiness, which are things you rather need in a horror game about a detective.

The Sinking City 2 wisely bins most of that, and is instead pretty much pure survival horror in a series of constrained locations. It's Resident Evil right down to puzzle locks and zombies who sometimes come back stronger after being shot, only set in the 1920s. Which is no bad thing. Resident Evil: Roaring '20s Revelations is a solid videogame pitch, and now we don't have to wait for Capcom to make it.

Arkham—the city from Lovecraft's stories, not the asylum where Batman locks up Condiment King—has flooded, which is a problem for many people, but notably for hat-wearing occult adventurer Calvin Rafferty. A brand new protagonist, the only references to the original Sinking City in this sequel being easter eggs, Cal's out to revive his partner in occult adventure and also life, Faye Bennett. She's in a supernatural coma after a trip to the Dreamlands.

The Sinking City 2 is a confident adventure that can go tentacle to tentacle with modern survival horror like Resident Evil and Silent Hill. The odd misstep is forgiven when Lovecraftian twists work so well to deliver some unsettling, unexpected moments of terror that just feel oh so joyous to squeal at.

I've unwisely let my inventory fill up, even as The Sinking City 2 bleeds my ammunition. I'm back-tracking, but the road back to the safe room is long, and more writhing, water-logged, bloated undead lunge at me through half-flooded spaces than were there previously. Before I can make it to safety and combine resources from my item box to concoct more ammunition or healing items, a new enemy type unceremoniously appears and throws me across the room. Screaming, I unload any remaining bullets into whichever part of its fishy skin looks to be a weak spot. The Sinking City 2 truly has the survival horror juice to be in conversation with modern Resident Evil and Silent Hill entries.

The Sinking City 2 is clearly influenced by both those horror series. At times, it feels like a love letter to iconic survival horror moments, and it wisely lifts some of their best features – from Resident Evil 2 remake 's color-coded maps for the item-hungry, to an early section set in the flooded streets of Arkham that reminds me of wandering through Silent Hill 2 remake 's urban early hours. Inventory management, safe rooms, and item boxes are present – including crafting recipes that share resources between ammo and health, meaning you have to make agonizing decisions about what you most need to press further into the unknown. Yet, The Sinking City 2 uses its Lovecraftian, cosmic horror theming to push beyond its contemporaries.

I've been fascinated by survival horror since the first Silent Hill on PS1, though these days I'm only slightly less of a scaredy cat. I also really like Frogwares' Sherlock Holmes games, and enjoyed the first The Sinking City. Recently, I've been putting a lot of time into the excellent Resident Evil Requiem and Silent Hill f. Using a PS5 code from the publisher, my first The Sinking City 2 playthrough took just under 10 hours, and I've been noodling with post-game content since then. - Reviewer Oscar Taylor-Kent
Release date: August 18, 2026 Platform(s): PC, PS5, Xbox Series X Developer: In-house Publisher: Frogwares

So much of what makes the best survival horror games great, after all – is the not knowing. It's what made considering when to use the titular gun in Resident Evil Requiem such a thrill in its early hours, after all. Yet, I'm now so familiar with Resident Evil and Silent Hill games that even in new entries I largely know what to expect.

reviews.title: Review: The Sinking City 2 (PS5) - An Admirable Resident Evil-Lite Experience
reviews.identity_evidence: Direct registered professional publisher review verified for The Sinking City 2.
evidence_points: For over a decade now, the Ukrainian developer Frogwares has been expanding and improving its Mind Palace mechanic. A feature that connects clues and forms conclusions, it’s spearheaded all the recent Sherlock Holmes games and The Sinking City — a solid set of investigative titles.
It’s probably what the studio is best known for, so to throw most of that work out and go in a new direction for The Sinking City 2 represents a bold move.

Frogwares is now doing survival horror of the Resident Evil and Silent Hill ilk, as it fashions a standalone sequel more about combat and puzzle-solving than analysis. It’s also considerably more linear and your actions have no impact on the story; the second game is almost the complete reverse of the original.
All these changes, updates, and decisions, however, have allowed Frogwares to elevate its craft: in The Sinking City 2, the team has its best achievement to date.

There are still some flaws, from stiff facial and voice performances to poor enemy variety, and the experience ultimately doesn’t reach the heights of bigger budget efforts. It’s still an admirable game, though, that presents something of a diet version of the Resident Evil formula through sound combat, exploration, and puzzles.

Despite the number in the title, The Sinking City 2 is unrelated to the first game, as Calvin Raffery claims the protagonist role for a quest to save his partner from a magical coma. Inspired by the works of author H. P. Lovecraft, the journey into Cthulhu mythos is set in 1920s Arkham and explores many of the themes and fantasies of the genre.

A flood has destroyed much of Arkham, forcing Calvin to travel from place to place by boat. Compared to the first game, boat travel is far less pronounced; it’s simply a vehicle to get you from one location to the next.

By taking value away from such a feature, it’s placed all the emphasis on the action on foot. The game is structured around visiting these storm-swept places, where you’ll encounter all the hallmarks of a survival horror classic: I’m talking weird puzzles, risky combat encounters, inventory and resource management, and special save rooms.

The puzzles are the highlight, requiring both a keen eye to connect clues and figure out answers from files, and a curious brain. Some involve decoding safe solutions while others demand you search the environment and probe and prod to reveal its secrets.

As a lover of all the strangest brain teasers from the Capcom and Konami classics, I think Frogwares has a fantastic set of puzzles to be proud of in The Sinking City 2. Like I said, the sequel feels like a lighter version of Resident Evil and Silent Hill, so at no point does it actually surpass the inspiration. However, what’s here is really, really good.

reviews.title: The Sinking City 2 Review – Drowned and out in Arkham | TheSixthAxis
reviews.identity_evidence: Direct registered professional publisher review verified for The Sinking City 2.
evidence_points: The original Sinking City was a title that found a cult following despite, or in some ways because of, its jankiness. Taking familiar Lovecraftian settings and themes and placing them in a semi-open world investigative game was an inspired decision and many players saw past the occasional bugs and flaws to find a thrilling and ambitious game. Since release, the title and its developers have endured numerous challenges from publisher fallouts to the literal invasion of their home country, so it is almost a miracle that the sequel has been finished at all. The fact that this second game is so much more polished and focused is even more remarkable.

Despite some visual similarities in tone and style, The Sinking City 2 is not a direct sequel in storyline or character. Charles Winfield Reed, the private investigator protagonist from the first game has been replaced by Calvin Rafferty, a figure more versed in the supernatural than his predecessor, but still a similar character in many ways. The story begins in media res as Calvin must discover the details of a ritual that will bring his partner, Faye Bennett, back from a mysterious coma. As the game progresses this narrative develops, with some interesting chronological twists and turns as well as some morally grey decisions (albeit with less of the choice from the original). Calvin is a likeable protagonist but feels more in keeping with classic survival horror than investigation.

Playing on PS5, The Sinking City 2 performs well, with very few frame drops that I noticed on the 60fps Performance preset. The Quality setting felt unplayable, however, as the extra fancy lighting tanked the frame rate, so consider this strictly for Pro owners only. Areas are well designed and have distinct aesthetics from the tight corridors of a disused hospital to the more expansive environment of an Antarctic expedition. Facial animation isn’t the most advanced, but is more than adequate to accompany the very strong voice acting and audio design in general.

Whereas the original game was a flawed but ambitious cult favourite, The Sinking City 2 is a far more focused and polished affair. Gone are the open world aspects, with a more linear progression along the flooded streets of Arkham and beyond and no requirement to use investigation mechanics to reveal objectives. This may prove to be a controversial decision as it does remove much of the unique character of the original in favour of a more traditional survival horror experience. Fortunately the more linear gameplay is designed well enough that it will appeal to fans of Resident Evil and the like.

While no longer a key gameplay mechanic, some aspects of the investigative horror original are maintained. The lore spread across each area in the form of notes and letters is split between background detail and puzzle solutions. Putting together the relevant clues in your journal rewards you with both in-game items and upgrade points for the passive bonuses applied through the new Talent Tables. Much of this can be ignored for those who want to focus on action, though, or equally those looking to speedrun subsequent playthroughs for challenges and trophies.

I was initially a little concerned about this change, that the consequence would be a more generic game without the unique character that made the original stand out. This is true up to a point, but once you take the game on its own terms then a highly enjoyable survival horror is revealed. Levels are well designed with multiple loops and shortcuts to unlock as you progress and the resource scarcity is well judged to ensure that you never feel completely safe or overpowered (unless playing on the easiest difficulty setting and using invincibility options).

Your initial loadout consists of a simple pistol that does decent damage, especially when you focus on the prominent enemy weak points. Later you’ll find the usual range of shotgun, rifle, and sub-machine gun, with each taking separate ammo and therefore needing inventory management. Exploring and solving all the puzzles is necessary to expand your very limited inventory and to find upgrade parts for each weapon. The final powerful weapon seemed unnecessary, however, and I left it in storage until the final boss of the game.

Each level is found through exploring the flooded streets of Arkham but there are practically no alternative paths or hidden areas to find. This makes the boat sections feel like extended loading areas of past generations, rather than truly interactive parts of the game, but does mean there is less backtracking or potential to get lost, which the first game was overly prone to. Within each level you’ll be following the usual survival horror tropes of finding keys and unlocking paths with a sprinkle of environmental puzzles to solve. There are a couple of boss encounters but most of the time you’ll be fighting a relatively small range of enemy types.
